messages:
jen: Heads-up — ran a 24h long-context perf run and saw steady RSS growth tied to the KV cache. Not a leak in app code; looks allocator/fragmentation-y. attaching quick traces.

mike: Can you paste the allocator breakdown? was it small-chunk churn or big-slot retention?

jen: Small-chunk churn + pockets of >90% occupancy in some slots but they never get reclaimed. Snapshot from the sampling probe:

```text
kvcache:hot-allocs: 512 -> 1024 buckets (hotset)
avg_alloc_size: 1.6KB
free_frag_ratio_by_bucket: [0.05, 0.12, 0.40, 0.02, ...]
hotset_residency_ms > 86,000 (24h)
most-frequent-sizes: 128, 256, 384
``` 

sara: Huh. 384 is odd — we usually see powers-of-two. Are those from serialization padding or sub-block splits?

jen: Looks like sub-block splitting from our buddy-like mini-allocator inside each slab. The allocator is rounding up to 128 but then splitting to 384 when long ctx uses >1 cache entry per token seq.

profiling-bot: snapshot/1769998642 uploaded: flamegraph and heap-sample (link: https://internal.prod/prof/1769998642)

alan: What about eviction/paging thresholds? any forced compactions triggered?

jen: Eviction policy ran but couldn't find contiguous free runs to satisfy a handful of 384-sized requests, so it kept allocating more slabs. Evict counts spiked but reclaimed bytes << bytes allocated.

mike: So fragmentation -> allocation amplification -> slab growth. Two quick options:
1) change block size granularity (introduce 64/96 bucket sizes)
2) run a background coalescer that tries to merge adjacent free subblocks within a slab

sara: I'd prefer #2 if it's cheap. But we need to quantify scanning cost vs memory saved. Maybe sampling-driven compaction: only scan slabs with high scatter entropy.

jen: Agreed. Proposed heuristic: track per-slab reuse histogram for last N minutes. If free_frag_ratio > 30% and reuse_entropy < X and age > Y, enqueue for lightweight compaction. Compaction does in-place coalesce of adjacent free subblocks; full copy-compact only if net reclaim > threshold.

alan: Do we have a cheap way to compute reuse_entropy? maybe maintain a 64-bit bloom-ish heatmap updated on hits.

mike: Yeah, use a 64-slot ring counter per slab, increment on hit of slot idx%64, periodically decay. computes entropy cheaply.

jen: Here's a quick proto CLI I used to inspect candidates:

```bash
# list slabs flagged by sampling
rdw-kvcache-inspect --since=24h --samples=1m --flag-candidates

# sample output
SLAB 0x7f3a1af4 size=16MB free_frag=0.38 hotness=0.92 entropy=0.12 candidates=3
SLAB 0x7f3a9bf0 size=8MB free_frag=0.41 hotness=0.11 entropy=0.06 candidates=5
```

sara: That entropy=0.06 slab looks stale — good compaction target. Can we do compaction cooperatively on request threads to amortize cost?

jen: Plan: background coalescer does lightweight pass; when it finds a candidate, it marks slab read-only and lets in-flight ops finish, then steals a short CPU window to merge free neighbors. If merge yields >64KB reclaim, mark for eviction. Otherwise leave alone.

mike: Two more concerns: checkpointing (we need snapshots for private deployments) and correctness with concurrent KV ops. We'll need CAS semantics and a small epoch barrier for slab muting.

alan: Also consider adding a configurable small-chunk freelist that favors reusing exact sizes first to limit split/merge churn.

jen: Good call. Action items:
- jen: wire the 64-slot heatmap into sampling probe and surface slab candidates (I'll open a PR)
- mike: prototype the in-place coalescer state machine (can we reuse current GC thread?)
- sara: run 3 canary runs with compaction disabled/enabled/aggresive-blocksize-change and capture RSS + evict stats
- alan: review concurrency protocol for slab muting and CAS safety

sara: I can run the canaries tomorrow morning (EU). I'll post raw logs and a short summary.

jen: Thanks. Leaving this open for follow-ups — tagging @mike @alan @sara. :mag: If anyone else has similar long-context traces, please drop them here.

mike: I'll take the PR review once it's up. :+1:

profiling-bot: reminder: schedule perf-run stack at 2024-09-12T08:00Z

jen: cool — thanks all.
